title: Huawei convicted on 10 counts by US jury over Iran business and trade secrets; China objects
dek: A Brooklyn jury found the Chinese telecoms company guilty of bank fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets, but cleared it of racketeering. Beijing said it opposes the US 'suppressing' Chinese firms.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
A federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, has convicted Huawei Technologies and three of its subsidiaries on 10 of 12 criminal counts, including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and violating US sanctions on Iran, closing the main chapter of a case that has strained relations between Washington and Beijing since 2018.

The jury acquitted the company of the two remaining charges, racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice, when it returned its verdict on Tuesday, 24 November, US time. Judge Ann Donnelly has set sentencing for 14 September 2027. Because the defendant is a company, the penalties are fines, forfeiture and restitution; reports said their size was not yet clear. Huawei says it will appeal.

## The case

Prosecutors in the Eastern District of New York alleged that Huawei misled global banks about its business in Iran, run through a Hong Kong-registered company called Skycom, so that it could keep access to US-dollar clearing while supplying telecoms equipment to Iran. When the expanded indictment was announced in February 2020, the Justice Department said Huawei had falsely told banks it had sold Skycom when, in reality, "Huawei sold Skycom to itself".

The trade-secret counts concerned technology from US companies including T-Mobile, Cisco, Quintel and CNEX, according to reports of the trial. Reports differ on its length, describing it as lasting about two or three months.

"No person or company is above the law," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said after the verdict, according to reports. Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva said Huawei had "built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception" over two decades.

Huawei said in a statement on Wednesday that it welcomed the racketeering acquittal and that the remaining convictions were "equally without legal or factual merit". It said the trade-secret disputes cited at trial were civil matters that had already been resolved, and that it would take "all necessary legal actions" to defend its rights. Its lawyers argued in court that the banks knew about the Iran business and that prosecutors had cherry-picked isolated incidents.

## Beijing's response

China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, asked about the verdict at Wednesday's briefing in Beijing, said the Chinese government "firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises" and supports them in protecting their legitimate rights, according to reports. China did not announce any countermeasures.

The case began in public in December 2018, when Huawei's chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou, daughter of the company's founder, was arrested in Canada on a US warrant. China detained two Canadians days later. Meng returned to China in 2021 after reaching a deferred prosecution agreement in which she acknowledged that Huawei had concealed its Iran business; the two Canadians were released the same day. Huawei had been placed on a US trade blacklist in 2019.

## Why it matters for India

India has kept Huawei out of its 5G networks without naming it. In May 2021 the Department of Telecommunications approved 5G trials with Ericsson, Nokia, Samsung and the state-run C-DOT as equipment partners, leaving out Huawei and ZTE. Since June 2021, Indian operators may buy only from "trusted sources" approved by the government under a national security directive for the telecom sector.

The verdict, a court finding rather than an intelligence assessment, adds weight to the security concerns that underpin those rules. It comes as India weighs how far to rely on Chinese technology and parts elsewhere, from smartphones and solar panels to drone components, and as Washington presses partners to tighten their own controls on Chinese firms.
